source: The FEW HICCUPPS consistency oracles, by Michael Bolton and James Bach. Descriptions are ours.
about: Oracle seeds (issue #138): each one is a way to recognise a problem, and says which heuristics and which kinds of product fact it draws on. trailhound/ontology/seeder.py runs the heuristic library and a product's facts through them to build that product's oracle.

seeds.name: Claims
seeds.question: Does the product do what it claims? A claim is anything said about the product, by it or for it: specs and help text, the product's own pages and messages, marketing and website promotion, emails to customers, promises. Each one can be checked against what the product actually does.
seeds.fact_template: The product claims this, so it should hold: {fact}

seeds.name: Self-consistency
seeds.question: Compare two responses that should logically agree (e.g. same query, different path) for contradictions.
seeds.fact_template: Holds wherever the product shows it: {fact}

seeds.name: Comparable products
seeds.question: Does this system belong to a recognizable category of real-world systems? If so, what conventions or behaviors do systems in that category typically get right (or wrong) that this system should be checked against, even if never explicitly documented?
seeds.heuristic_template: Like other products of its kind, {entity} handles this: {description}

seeds.name: Dumb user
seeds.question: Would a naive user find this confusing or wrong, regardless of whether it's technically spec-compliant? Judge from the perspective of someone with no special knowledge of the system's internals or documentation.
seeds.heuristic_template: A user of {entity} would expect this: {description}

seeds.name: Statutes and standards
seeds.question: Does the product follow the laws, regulations and standards that apply to it, such as accessibility, privacy and security rules?

seeds.name: World
seeds.question: Does the product agree with how the real world works: dates, units, addresses, names, arithmetic?
seeds.heuristic_template: On {entity}, values agree with the real world: {description}

seeds.name: Purpose
seeds.question: Does the behaviour serve what the product is for, and what the user is trying to do?
seeds.fact_template: The product does what it's for: {fact}

seeds.name: Familiarity
seeds.question: Is this a kind of problem you've seen in other products? Known bug patterns are worth checking for on purpose.
seeds.heuristic_template: A problem familiar from other products, looked for on {entity}: {description}

seeds.name: Image
seeds.question: Does the behaviour fit the image the organisation wants? Rude messages, sloppy text or odd visuals hurt it.
seeds.heuristic_template: On {entity}, nothing hurts the product's image: {description}

seeds.name: Statistical/trend
seeds.question: Does this deviate from the system's own past behavior, latency drift, error-rate creep, or other trends observable only by comparing against prior runs or history? Needs accumulated data across runs to be meaningful; not useful on a single, first-time pass.
seeds.standing: Behaviour matches what earlier runs recorded; a change from an earlier run is worth a look.

seeds.name: Explainability
seeds.question: Can you explain what the product just did? Behaviour nobody can explain is worth reporting even if it isn't clearly wrong.
seeds.standing: Every result can be explained in one sentence; one that can't is worth reporting even if it isn't clearly wrong.
